messages.subject: plotting longitudinal data
parts:
I have a question with regard to plotting longitudinal data.

Specifically, I would like to have the X-axis represent the occasion
(oc1-oc10), and the y-axis to represent the range along which exposure
to violence was measured on each occasion (scores ranges from 1-4).
Finally, I want the color of the data points or the lines connecting
the means across each occasion to be set to different groups in the
sample (e.g., gender).

I am having difficulty figuring out what the Y-axis variable will be
in the syntax given that the scores for exposure to violence are
reflected in the variable measured at each occasion is designated to
be on the X-axis.

This is the syntax I am working with:

etv <- ggplot(data = etv, aes(x = exp1-10, y = ? , color = gender))
+ geom_point()

It may be a problem with the data set. Here is the way it is set up:

id gender exp1 exp3 exp3 exp4
exp5 .................................................exp10
1 1002 0 3 4 3 NA NA NA
NA 49 51 43 NA
2 1003 0 4 2 3 2 3 2
3 43 47 41 45
3 1004 0 4 4 4 4 4 4
4 52 53 63 61
4 1005 0 3 3 2 2 3 3
3 52 51 53 52
5 1006 0 3 2 1 3 3 4
3 51 50 48 51
6 1007 1 4 3 3 4 NA NA
NA NA NA 53 NA

exp1-10 represent each occasion in which exposure was assessed.

Do I need to create a new vector to represent occasion? And if so,
what do I do with exp1-10?

Thanks in advance for your time and assitance!

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: plotting longitudinal data
parts:
Hi:

You don't make it easy to help, but here's one stab at it.

Caveats:
(i) You said the exposure levels were 1-4, but you have four
variables whose values are all over 10 also labeled as 'expxx', where
xx is a number.
(ii) You repeated the same variable name twice.
I just retained the (seven) variables whose values were between 1 and
4, along with the id and gender variables.

Calling the read-in data frame DF, the trick is to melt the data so
that the occasions become a single (factor) variable and their
corresponding values a separate variable named 'value'. The melt()
function is in package reshape2. Next, I used the ddply() function
from the plyr package to get group/occasion means, but there are other
ways to do the same task that returns a data frame. The two resulting
data frames were then used as input to ggplot2 in separate layers.

library('ggplot2')
library('reshape2')
library('plyr')

# Keeps the first 9 variables, using the first two as ID variables
DFm <- melt(DF[, 1:9], id = 1:2)
# Convert gender to factor - use levels() to define M and F
# because you didn't mention it in your post
DFm$gender <- factor(DFm$gender)

# Find the occasion/gender means:
DFmsumm <- ddply(DFm, .(gender, variable), summarise,
emean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

# Now plot:
ggplot(DFm, aes(x = as.numeric(variable), y = value, colour = gender)) +
geom_point(size = 3,
position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2)) +
geom_line(data = DFmsumm,
aes(x = as.numeric(variable), y = emean), size = 1) +
labs(x = 'Occasion', y = 'Level of violence')

The occasion variable is coerced to numeric so that one is plotting
occasion number; it is also easier to plot lines when the x-variable
is numeric. The points were jittered in both the horizontal and
vertical directions to avoid overplotting.

BTW, this is a preferred way of sending data to an R-related news list
by e-mail:

> dput(DF)
structure(list(id = 1002:1007, gender = c(0L, 0L, 0L, 0L, 0L,
1L), exp01 = c(3L, 4L, 4L, 3L, 3L, 4L), exp02 = c(4L, 2L, 4L,
3L, 2L, 3L), exp03 = c(3L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 1L, 3L), exp04 = c(NA,
2L, 4L, 2L, 3L, 4L), exp05 = c(NA, 3L, 4L, 3L, 3L, NA), exp06 = c(NA,
2L, 4L, 3L, 4L, NA), exp07 = c(NA, 3L, 4L, 3L, 3L, NA), exp08 = c(49L,
43L, 52L, 52L, 51L, NA), exp09 = c(51L, 47L, 53L, 51L, 50L, NA
), exp10 = c(43L, 41L, 63L, 53L, 48L, 53L), exp11 = c(NA, 45L,
61L, 52L, 51L, NA)), .Names = c("id", "gender", "exp01", "exp02",
"exp03", "exp04", "exp05", "exp06", "exp07", "exp08", "exp09",
"exp10", "exp11"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -6L
))

In this form, useRs can copy and paste the output above into their own
R session (assigned to a variable name) and be assured that the data
they see in their sessions are the same as what you have in yours. In
contrast, there is no such guarantee when copying and pasting raw
output. For example, I had to convert gender from numeric to factor;
it is also possible that I may have needed to do that with id had the
occasion arisen. dput() eliminates the need for post-fixes.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: plotting longitudinal data
parts: Hi Tamim,

On Fri, May 11, 2012 at 6:48 PM, Tamim <tamimm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Dennis,
>
> Thanks so much for your help. The suggestions and steps you described
> culminated in an ideal plot of the longitudinal data.
>
> Below, I have pasted the entire output from the dput() function.
>
> What I would like to do now is add and modify a few things in the
> plot. Specifically, I would like to map some additional information
> (e.g., distribution of scores, confidence intervals) within each
> occasion on rate of exposure, as well as whether scores of exposure
> between occasions are significantly different from one another. Are
> these tasks relatively feasible?

Yes, just use the same technique you used for adding the lines:
calculate the upper and lower confidence intervals use e.g.,
geom_errorbar to plot them.

Also, I know the gender is mapped to
> color, but I am wondering if I can select the colors to be Black and
> Grey rather than Green and Orange.
Use scale_color_grey()

Finally, is there a way for the X-
> axes to specify Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, and Nine rather
> than the numbers 1-7. I tried using the scale_x_discrete() option,
> specifying breaks and labels, but it did not work.

You didn't tell us what the error message was, but notice that x is
numeric, so you probably need

scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 4, 6), labels = c("two", "four", "six"))

Best,
Ista
